channel.title: whataifound.org: What AI Has Actually Contributed
channel.description: New and updated entries in the whataifound.org registry of AI contributions to science and mathematics, graded on verification and autonomy.

item.title: Randomised trial of voice-guided AI navigation for biliopancreatic endoscopic ultrasound
item.description: In a single-centre randomised trial of 266 patients in China, a real-time AI system that recognises scanning stations and prompts the endoscopist by voice raised the completeness of guideline-recommended biliopancreatic endoscopic ultrasound stations from a median of 0.81 to 1.00, while lengthening procedures by about two minutes. EUS-GUIDEQ was developed from 27,072 annotated images from 189 patients, with station classification accuracy of 94.2% on 1,500 internal images and 78.8% on 2,062 multicentre external images. Between December 2023 and May 2025 patients were randomised 1:1 to AI-assisted or standard examination, with 132 and 134 analysed. The primary endpoint, completeness of standardised scanning stations adjudicated by blinded experts from recorded video, was a median of 1.00 (interquartile range 0.94 to 1.00) against 0.81 (0.75 to 0.88), P < 0.001, with benefit across participating endoscopists. Procedure time was 12.70 against 10.55 minutes, and no serious procedure-related adverse events occurred. Lab: Central South University (Third Xiangya Hospital). Model: EUS-GUIDEQ. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Weak normalization implies strong normalization in pure type systems with βη-conversion, proved in Lean
item.description: A Lean proof, written by Claude Opus 5.5 under four authors' direction by adapting OpenAI's proof of the β case, that in every pure type system with βη-conversion, if every legal term is weakly normalizing then every legal term is strongly normalizing, the βη form of a conjecture Geuvers stated in 1993. The Barendregt-Geuvers-Klop conjecture asks whether weak normalization implies strong normalization in every pure type system; Geuvers states it for all of them in his 1993 thesis as Conjecture 8.1.2. OpenAI's release of 6 October 2026 included a preprint and Lean proof of the case where the conversion rule uses β-conversion only, family 245 of the collection recorded at 2026-10-06-openai-math-collection. This development proves the βη case for every specification, with no functionality, finiteness or decidability assumed: weak βη-normalization of every legal term implies strong βη-normalization, and so does weak β-normalization. Because an η-step can delete a λ-annotation, the proof works from the weaker property that every legal term has a β-reduct with no β-redex outside its λ-domains, handles conversion through domain erasure, indexes candidates by βη-normal forms of erased types and makes observation values η-canonical. OpenAI's 33 Lean files for the β case are copied in and ported to Lean v4.35.0. Lab: Independent. Model: Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, adapting an OpenAI Lean proof of the β case. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: Measurably isomorphic Bernoulli shifts with different base entropies, proved in Lean
item.description: A Lean proof, registered on Palomar, that some countable group has measurably isomorphic Bernoulli shifts over alphabets of different sizes, so that base entropy is not an isomorphism invariant for that group; the group comes from OpenAI's claimed counterexample to Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture, and the dynamical construction was written with GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Sol under Peter Burton's direction. For a countable group G and a finite alphabet A, the Bernoulli shift is G acting by translation on A^G with the uniform product measure. Ornstein showed in 1970 that base entropy is a complete invariant of these shifts over the integers, and Bowen showed in 2010 that it is an isomorphism invariant over every sofic group, so shifts with different base entropies can be isomorphic only over a group outside that class. The registered theorem gives a countable group G and a nontrivial finite alphabet A for which the shifts on A and on A × A are equivariantly isomorphic on invariant conull sets, with a measurable inverse. The group and the algebraic input come from OpenAI's manuscript A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Characteristic Two, whose abstract says the group is non-sofic; its Lean development is imported at a pinned commit, and this project builds the dynamical conjugacy on top of it. Lab: Independent. Model: GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Sol via Codex, building on an OpenAI construction. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: System-wide AI scribe deployment and clinician documentation time at a 14-hospital health system
item.description: Across 1,637,227 outpatient encounters at a 14-hospital Boston health system, enrolment in the Heidi ambient AI scribe was associated with 1.21 fewer minutes of active note time per encounter, more among heavy users, and longer notes, with no change in same-day or after-hours note closure or in work relative value units. After system-wide availability from January 2025, 902 outpatient clinicians enrolled, of whom 605 used the tool and 297 did not. The study used an interrupted time series indexed on each clinician's enrolment month and adjusted for patient demographics and visit complexity, over notes from 1 July 2024 to 31 January 2026, with a secondary comparison of non-users, low users and high users. Note-active time fell by 1.21 minutes (95% CI 0.68 to 1.74) on enrolment and by 2.50 minutes among high users, and high users' notes grew by about 171 characters relative to non-users. Lab: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Beth Israel Lahey Health. Model: Heidi (Heidi Health). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Classification of Finite Simple Groups formalized in Lean by directed AI agents
item.description: Axiom Math released a sorry-free Lean proof of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups that follows the first-generation proof, about 43.1 million lines written over 24 days by swarms of AI agents directed by its mathematicians and engineers, whose agents also found counterexamples to a step in one published route to the Unbalanced Group Theorem. The classification states that every finite simple group is cyclic of prime order, alternating, of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups. Its first-generation proof is spread over hundreds of papers and books, and the second-generation revision is incomplete, so the project formalized the first-generation proof. The README states the theorem through the classification statement of the TauCeti project, written outside Axiom, and says the proof builds on Mathlib and TauCeti with only Lean's three standard axioms and no native_decide. The announcement says about 1.2 million lines come from the Qiuzhen-CFSG project and that the work was split into 108 milestones and about 380 tasks, with lead agents decomposing arguments and reviewing the statements being formalized while other agents searched for existing results or wrote proofs. Formalizing Walter's argument, the agents found explicit counterexamples to a closure assertion it uses, and a companion paper by Colin Defant and Ken Ono gives an alternative argument for the simple-group case of the Unbalanced Group Theorem built on Solomon's 1976 theory of maximal 2-components, whose key step the announcement credits to AxiomProver. Lab: Axiom Math. Model: AxiomProver agent system using an unnamed, changing mix of models. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: Sogge's local smoothing conjecture claimed in every dimension, with Bochner–Riesz and Kakeya as consequences
item.description: An OpenAI manuscript released with a Lean formalization claims Sogge's local smoothing conjecture for the wave equation in every spatial dimension, and from it the Bochner–Riesz conjecture, the Kakeya and Nikodym maximal conjectures, full Hausdorff dimension for every Euclidean Kakeya set, and Fourier restriction for the sphere, paraboloid and cone throughout the interior of the conjectured range. Local smoothing asks how much regularity solutions of the wave equation gain on average in time beyond what fixed-time estimates allow. Sogge conjectured the sharp form in 1991, and it was known to imply the Bochner–Riesz and Kakeya conjectures; Guth, Wang and Zhang proved it in two spatial dimensions in 2020. Family 079 of openai/math, added on 26 October 2026, pairs a manuscript dated 25 October with an earlier one claiming the critical L³ estimate in three dimensions. OpenAI's scope page says the Lean formalization bounds, for every n ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ p < ∞, the Lᵖ(ℝⁿ × [1, 2]) norm of the half-wave by the W^(s, p) norm of Schwartz initial data with s = max(0, (n − 1)/2 − n/p) + ε, and also gives uniform Bochner–Riesz bounds, spherical extension estimates and Stein square-function bounds in their strict ranges, the Kakeya maximal bound with δ^(−ε) loss, and full dimension for every set containing a unit segment in each direction. The release note says the model output is published directly, as in the release of 6 October. Lab: OpenAI. Model: Unreleased internal OpenAI model, not named in the release. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Deep learning detection and staging of femoral head osteonecrosis on hip x-rays across six Chinese hospitals
item.description: OsteoAID, a YOLOv8-based model trained on 20,722 hip x-rays from 16,399 patients at six Chinese hospitals, staged osteonecrosis of the femoral head with 96.6% accuracy on an external test set, against 75.0% for radiologists. Expert orthopaedists annotated each image to separate osteonecrosis from radiographically similar conditions and graded confirmed lesions on the Ficat and Arlet scale, using images from 2015 to 2023. On the internal test set the model raised staging accuracy from 87.4% for the unmodified YOLOv8 network to 96.4%, with a detection mean average precision of 93.0% at an intersection-over-union threshold of 50%. It was compared with radiologists and orthopaedists on two external test sets, and with MRI-based staging, the reference standard, on a third. The authors propose it as a decision-support tool for triage. Lab: Sun Yat-sen University (with the Chinese Artificial Intelligence Project Group for Hip Joint Diseases). Model: OsteoAID (YOLOv8-based). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Multiagent language-model and CNN system scores BT-RADS on glioma follow-up MRI
item.description: A system pairing a locally run 20-billion-parameter gpt-oss model, which extracts clinical variables from notes, with a scoring agent applying BT-RADS logic to tumour volumetrics classified 492 post-treatment glioma MRI examinations with 76.0% accuracy against an expert reference, against 57.5% for the initial clinical assessments. BT-RADS standardises response assessment after glioma treatment but requires combining imaging trends with medication effects and radiation timing. 509 consecutive examinations from 2017 to 2021 at one centre were evaluated retrospectively, 492 of them evaluable. Agreement with the reference had a Cohen kappa of 0.71. Sensitivity was high in categories that depend on clinical context (100% for BT-1b, 92.7% for BT-1a, 87.5% for BT-3a) and moderate in those that depend on thresholds (57.1% to 74.8%), and positive predictive value for BT-4 was 92.9%. Lab: Duke University Medical Center. Model: gpt-oss 20B (OpenAI, open weights) extractor agent with a convolutional neural network scorer. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Chest radiograph model for prescreening reduced ejection fraction, tested in three Korean cohorts
item.description: DLLV, a deep learning model that flags a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% or less on chest radiographs, reached AUCs of 0.86 in a tertiary-centre cohort and 0.92 to 0.97 in two health-checkup cohorts, and as a prescreen was estimated to cut echocardiography volume by up to 85% without missing any of the 19 affected people in those cohorts. The model was developed on 24,674 patients with 32,135 same-day radiograph and echocardiogram pairs from 2016 to 2021, using counterfactual learning to improve performance and the localisation of its heatmaps. External testing covered a tertiary referral cohort of 5,440 patients and two health-checkup cohorts of 28,034 and 6,085. In the checkup cohorts the area under the precision-recall curve was 0.04, which still corresponds to 87-fold and 37-fold enrichment over the low baseline prevalence. Lab: Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. Model: DLLV. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: ECG deep learning ensemble separates Takotsubo syndrome from anterior STEMI and improves reader accuracy
item.description: A preprint reports an ensemble of three deep learning models that distinguished Takotsubo syndrome from acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction on 12-lead ECG images with 91.4% accuracy in a 95-person external cohort, and raised 70 healthcare providers' estimated probability of a correct diagnosis from 0.632 unaided to 0.864 with AI assistance. The models were pretrained self-supervised and fine-tuned on ECG images from two hospitals recorded within 14 days of symptom onset, with 832 participants for development and 95 for external validation, healthy controls included. External AUROC was 0.970. A four-phase reader study compared unaided reading, a reference sheet and AI assistance, then randomised readers on a new ECG set to the reference sheet alone, AI predictions, or AI predictions with Grad-CAM heatmaps, which gave a further gain. In exploratory analyses less experienced readers gained most, and cardiologists' unaided advantage reversed under AI assistance, which the authors frame as a utilisation bias hypothesis. Lab: North Medical Center Hiroshima City Asa Citizens Hospital. Model: Ensemble of three deep learning models with self-supervised pretraining. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Épi agent reports 120 record bounds and constructions, with released certificates
item.description: Bake AI's Épi agent, running GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra against fixed verifiers, reports 20 improved numerical bounds and 100 record constructions, including certificates that the Cohn–Elkies sphere-packing bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11, an upper bound of 4.29569 on Klarner's polyomino growth constant against 4.5238, and a computer-assisted extension of Tuza's conjecture for a class of split graphs. Épi keeps a persistent research history across model sessions, branches and reviews its own work, and has each output scored by a fixed verifier, accepting an improvement only when it is feasible and clears a set margin over the literature value. The results repository lists 12 families of numerical bounds and 8 of constructions. The headline mathematics: dual certificates giving lower bounds on the Cohn–Elkies linear programme of about 0.0564 and 0.0577 in dimensions 10 and 11, above the known upper bounds on sphere-packing density there, so the method cannot be sharp in either; the bound λ ≤ 4.29569 for Klarner's constant, whose previous record was 4.5238 and whose empirical value is about 4.06; an interval for the n-queens constant about 84 times narrower than before; and a proof that τ_(△)(G) ≤ 2ν_(△)(G) for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three active neighbourhood types, up from two. The construction records are mostly circle and ball packings, 46 of them circles in a quarter disk. Lab: Bake AI. Model: GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra in the Épi agent. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: AI-enhanced auscultation for left ventricular dysfunction, validated in prospective Japanese cohorts
item.description: An AI model reading digital heart sounds from four chest sites with a single-lead ECG detected an ejection fraction of 40% or less with an AUROC of 0.904 in an external prospective cohort of 964 patients, and was more accurate than a consensus of seven cardiologists in a 100-patient reader substudy (82.0% against 62.0%). Adults referred for clinically indicated echocardiography at multiple Japanese centres underwent digital auscultation with a simultaneous single-lead ECG, with same-visit echocardiography as the reference. The ensemble was trained on 2,359 patients, 8.9% with reduced ejection fraction, and validated on 964 from a separate multicentre registry, 7.6% with it. External sensitivity, specificity and accuracy were 86.3%, 74.2% and 75.1%. The model outperformed ECG-only models and clinical regression models including B-type natriuretic peptide, and a simplified two-site version kept an AUROC of 0.903. Lab: Juntendo University (with AMI Inc.). Model: Transformer and one-dimensional CNN ensemble over four-site digital auscultation and single-lead ECG. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: RFdiffusion3 designs active phosphotriesterases and transthyretin-specific zinc proteases zero-shot
item.description: RFdiffusion3, a generative model that diffuses free atoms to satisfy atomic constraints, produced de novo phosphotriesterases with a two-metal active site and zinc proteases specific for transthyretin, obtaining active catalysts of both kinds from zero-shot design campaigns of 96 constructs. The method places individual atoms rather than residues, aiming to meet sets of atomic constraints such as an enzyme active site more quickly and accurately than earlier methods, across tasks from enzyme design to RNA structure design. The experimental demonstrations are two enzyme classes: phosphotriesterases whose active site includes a carbamylated lysine coordinating two metal ions, and zinc proteases that cut transthyretin, the protein involved in transthyretin amyloid disease. In both, a campaign of 96 constructs tested without iterative optimisation yielded active catalysts. Lab: Institute for Protein Design, University of Washington. Model: RFdiffusion3. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: Randomised trial of AI-generated lay summaries before neurosurgical consultations
item.description: In a single-centre randomised trial of 300 outpatients in Dresden, giving patients a quality-checked AI-generated lay summary of their medical findings before consultation improved patient-rated quality of the physician-patient interaction (4.42 against 4.25 on the FAPI scale) and shortened median consultations from 33 to 25 minutes. Adults attending an outpatient neurosurgical clinic were randomised 1:1 to standard care with or without a layperson summary of their findings, produced by the Simply Onno tool and quality-checked before use. The primary endpoint, patient-reported interaction quality, improved by 0.17 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.29), driven by shared decision-making, with no difference in perceived empathy. Patients rated autonomy support higher while physicians rated their own slightly lower, and the ratio of geometric mean consultation times was 0.79 (0.70 to 0.88). Evidence for an increase in encounter difficulty was weak, and secondary intervals were not adjusted for multiplicity. Lab: TU Dresden (University Hospital Carl Gustav Carus). Model: Simply Onno (underlying model not named in the abstract). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Integer multiplication below n log n, against the Schönhage–Strassen optimality conjecture
item.description: An OpenAI manuscript gives a deterministic algorithm that multiplies two n-bit integers in time O(n(log n)^(1 − κ)) with κ = 2⁻¹⁸² on a multitape Turing machine, which would beat the O(n log n) algorithm of Harvey and van der Hoeven and disprove Schönhage and Strassen's 1971 conjecture that n log n is optimal; David Harvey calls the claim plausible but says he has not checked it. Schönhage and Strassen conjectured in 1971 that multiplying n-bit integers needs on the order of n log n bit operations, and Harvey and van der Hoeven reached that bound in 2021. Family 109 of OpenAI's release claims an algorithm running in O(n(log n)^(1 − κ)) with κ = 2⁻¹⁸², exact at every input length on one fixed finite-alphabet Turing machine with finitely many one-dimensional tapes. The manuscript is dated 23 September 2026 and was published with the release of 6 October. Harvey's note of 20 October describes three closely related manuscripts, says the work builds directly on the 2021 algorithm, and reports that others had already lowered the exponent of log n to about 0.9983. He argues that the size of κ is beside the point, since saving a power of log n is exponentially larger than any earlier improvement in this line. Lab: OpenAI. Model: Unreleased internal OpenAI model, not named in the release. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Locked AI model for p16/Ki-67 dual-stain triage validated on 9,006 cervical screening cases
item.description: Cytoreader-Fusion, an AI system that classifies p16/Ki-67 dual-stain cytology slides to triage HPV-positive screening results, was locked before validation and then detected biopsy-confirmed CIN 3+ with 88.3% sensitivity and 54.4% specificity in a held-out cohort of 4,996 cases. Dual-stain cytology is the guideline-endorsed triage for HPV-positive screening results but depends on manual reading. The ensemble model was trained on 1,919 cases and evaluated under blinded honest-broker oversight on 9,006 cases in four cohorts, with all preprocessing, aggregation rules and decision parameters fixed before validation. The endpoint was histologically confirmed CIN 3+, or AIN 3+ in an anal cohort, rather than agreement with cytologists, and one classifier served both ThinPrep and SurePath slides without retraining. In the post-lock cohort sensitivity was 88.3% (90% interval 85.3 to 91.3) and specificity 54.4% (52.9 to 55.9); across cohorts the authors report both above ASC-US+ Pap cytology and comparable to or exceeding manual dual-stain reading. Lab: University Medicine Göttingen (with H-Labs and the US National Cancer Institute). Model: Cytoreader-Fusion. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Eight open problems from Formal Conjectures proved in Lean by a simple agent loop
item.description: A team at FAIR at Meta ran GPT-5.6 Sol in h1, a minimal loop that gives a model a Lean interface and verifier feedback, on 236 problems listed as open in Google DeepMind's Formal Conjectures repository and obtained Lean proofs of eight of them, among them a variant of Erdős Problem 337, three OEIS conjectures and the existence of an AME(9, 10) quantum state; Formal Conjectures marked five as solved. The eight are: W(k)/2ᵏ → ∞ for two-colour van der Waerden numbers, a variant of Erdős 138; the Ruzsa-Turjányi variant of Erdős 337, that |(A + A) ∩ [1, 2N]|/|A ∩ [1, N]| → ∞ for every asymptotic basis of density zero; the OEIS conjectures for A108081, A211417 (Bala's supercongruence, p³ᵏ|a(pᵏ) − a(p^(k − 1)) for primes p ≥ 5) and A022030; the existence of an AME(9, 10) state, a unit vector in (ℂ¹⁰)^(⊗9) whose reduction to any four parties is maximally mixed, which is Open Quantum Problem 35; and Written on the Wall II Conjectures 100 and 314. The proofs were made public on 2026-09-14 in a pull request to Formal Conjectures, merged on 2026-09-24, that marks the first five as solved with links to a repository of nine Lean files; the ninth, Green's Open Problem 25, is not counted in the paper. The paper, dated 28 October 2026, also reports that the loop exposed several misformalizations in Formal Conjectures by proving short disproofs of the written statements, including a smooth four-dimensional Poincaré variant missing a Hausdorff hypothesis. Lab: FAIR at Meta. Model: GPT-5.6 Sol in the h1 harness. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: A shortened CAR intracellular domain designed with Claude Code
item.description: Six scientists at Generate Biomedicines used Claude Code to propose new designs for the intracellular signalling region of a CAR T-cell receptor; one design was about 70 percent shorter than the standard version and, in cell assays, let immune cells display roughly 10 times as many receptors, kill tumour cells more efficiently and stay active longer, with no animal or patient data reported. CAR T-cell therapy has mostly treated cancers of the blood cells, and Generate Biomedicines is trying to reengineer it to treat solid tumours as well. Its approach is to shorten one part of the therapy's genetic instructions so that there is room for further instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for that part, and one proposal was about 70 percent shorter than the standard version. In laboratory tests that design beat the standard on three measures at once: immune cells made roughly 10 times as many receptors, the proteins they use to spot cancer cells, they killed tumour cells more efficiently, and they stayed active for longer. The announcement reports no animal work and no clinical work, and gives no affinities, replicate counts or statistics. Lab: Generate Biomedicines / Anthropic. Model: Not disclosed; Claude accessed through Claude Code, with no model name or version given in the announcement. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Claude-generated antibody designs that dislodge receptor-bound IgE
item.description: Claude turned Divergence Labs' goals into a design plan and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month towards a two-armed treatment for food allergy; early testing found three designs that bound IgE and 20 that dislodged it from immune cells, three of the 20 appearing to dislodge more of it than the standard medication, and the two arms have not been combined into a single molecule. Food allergy is set off by IgE, some of it circulating free in the blood and some attached to the surface of immune cells. Standard medication neutralises the circulating IgE only. Divergence Labs is pursuing a molecule with two arms, one that binds IgE tightly and one that prises IgE off the immune cell, so that receptor-bound IgE is removed as well. Claude converted that goal into a detailed design plan and then generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs over about a month, which Divergence narrowed down and tested. The announcement reports hits for both arms, three designs that bound IgE and 20 that dislodged it, with three of the 20 appearing to dislodge more IgE than the standard medication. It gives no affinities, no assay format and no count of how many designs were tested to reach those hits. The stated next step, building one drug that combines the two arms, has not been done. Lab: Divergence Labs / Anthropic. Model: Not disclosed; no model name or version given in the announcement. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: Antibody fragment leads optimised with Claude on affinity, stability and aggregation
item.description: Claude, connected to BigHat Biosciences' laboratory data system, proposed changes to two antibody-fragment drug leads and BigHat's automated laboratory made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks; against the originals the best versions bound more than 10 times more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution at a temperature 18 degrees Celsius higher, and the lead meant to keep a drug in the body longer aggregated more than 100 times more slowly. A drug lead has to bind its target tightly, survive manufacturing and storage, and not clump together. BigHat Biosciences pairs machine learning with an automated laboratory to improve such leads. Its scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude on two antibody fragments, one aimed at cancer cells and one intended to keep a drug in the body longer, and Claude, connected to BigHat's laboratory data system Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule. The laboratory made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team came to suspect that the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading; Claude and the researcher reanalysed the raw data and proposed different metrics along with a protocol change to test them, and BigHat's scientists refined and ran that protocol, after which the announcement reports that the main predictions held. Against the original leads, the best versions bound more than 10 times more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution at a temperature 18 degrees Celsius higher, and the longer-lasting lead aggregated more than 100 times more slowly. Lab: BigHat Biosciences / Anthropic. Model: Not disclosed; no model name or version given in the announcement. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: A subexponential algorithm for counting 3-SAT solutions, refuting the Exponential Time Hypothesis
item.description: A 49-page paper authored by Claude gives a deterministic algorithm that counts the satisfying assignments of a 3-CNF formula on n variables in 2ᵒ⁽ⁿ⁾ time, which contradicts the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and a Lean 4 development in Anthropic's public repository states and proves the refutation against Mathlib's Turing machines using only Lean's three standard axioms. The Exponential Time Hypothesis of Impagliazzo and Paturi says there is a constant δ > 0 for which 3-SAT on n variables cannot be solved in O(2^δn) time. The paper gives a deterministic algorithm for the harder counting problem #3-SAT running in 2ᵒ⁽ⁿ⁾ time, which contradicts it, and a main theorem covering k-CNF formulas with m clauses in time 2^(O(min{km/√(log m), k²n log log n/√(log n)})). Every earlier improvement had reduced the exponent by a constant factor rather than removed it: the records the paper cites are O(1.328ⁿ) for deterministic 3-SAT and O(1.308ⁿ) for randomized. The paper states consequences for other NP-complete problems, with Independent Set, Clique, Vertex Cover and Dominating Set on n vertices each solvable in O(2^δn) time for every δ > 0. It says the result was found by an internal Claude research model using 14 million output tokens with no human input, after which Anthropic researchers worked with Claude on the presentation, and it names OpenAI's concurrent result as independent. The Lean development reached the public repository as pull request 31, merged on 27 October 2026 at commit 16a5ce41304fcdaea4e0be7c132e1c361dc26da5 and adding 1,063 files; the README documents a roughly eight-minute build on 24 virtual CPUs, pins Lean and Mathlib at v4.33.1, and prints the axiom dependencies of both headline theorems as exactly propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. Lab: Anthropic. Model: Unreleased internal Anthropic research model, not named or versioned; the paper's author line is Claude. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: A subexponential counting algorithm for fixed-width CNF, refuting the Exponential Time Hypothesis
item.description: A 67-page preprint authored by OpenAI gives a deterministic algorithm that exactly counts the satisfying assignments of a k-CNF formula in subexponential time and polynomial space, refuting the Exponential Time Hypothesis in the case of 3-SAT; OpenAI released it with a Lean formalization of a weaker bound than the manuscript claims, and announced that an independent working group of complexity theorists would examine the proof. For every fixed k ≥ 2 the preprint gives a deterministic algorithm that computes the exact number of satisfying assignments of a k-CNF on n variables and m clauses in polyₖ(n, m) space and time (n + m)^(Oₖ(1))2^(n/(log n)^(1/2 + o(1))). Since testing whether that count exceeds zero decides satisfiability, the case k = 3 contradicts the Exponential Time Hypothesis. The manuscript is dated 17 October 2026 and revised 25 October 2026, and its stated techniques are exact counting, sparse parity tests and polynomial interpolation. It was published on 26 October 2026 into openai/math, the repository of 721 manuscripts in 373 families that this registry already records at 2026-10-06-openai-math-collection, whose README frames the manuscripts as raw research data rather than polished papers and reports roughly 42 percent of top-line results formalized. The release note says an independent working group of computer scientists led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi and Ryan Williams will examine and explain the proof, and that OpenAI made the materials public immediately at the group's request. Lab: OpenAI. Model: Unreleased internal OpenAI model, not named in the release. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: PHP2Shell: two critical PHP remote code execution flaws found with AI assistance
item.description: Two security teams working independently, each using frontier language models to review PHP's source, found two unauthenticated remote code execution flaws in the runtime behind a large share of the web; both were rated 9.2 critical, and PHP shipped patches on 2026-10-21 under coordinated disclosure. The two flaws are separate root causes in PHP's request lifecycle. CVE-2026-109618, which PHP titles "RCE via OOM corruption", turns on PHP using longjmp() to abandon a request on an out-of-memory error: some contexts leave request memory uninitialized before an allocation, the cleanup that follows reads or branches on it, and the advisory states that multiple out-of-memory strategies trigger this consistently enough to reach remote code execution. CVE-2026-109619, "RCE via stale global state", covers global state that temporarily points into request memory and is then either not reset or repopulated after being reset, so a later request reads or branches on a pointer into memory that has been freed. Both carry a CVSS 4.0 base score of 9.2, neither needs authentication, and both were patched on 2026-10-21 in PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. The two teams arrived separately: Calif dates its discovery to 1 August 2026, reported the first flaw to PHP on 11 August and shared a working proof of concept that PHP confirmed on 15 August, while Wiz discovered its first on 19 August and reported on 24 August, with public disclosure held until the patched releases were out. Lab: Calif / Wiz Research / OpenAI. Model: Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, with the Wiz Atlas tool; which model did what differs by source, see caveats. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Lean formalization of the L³ bound for the trilinear Hilbert transform
item.description: An independent mathematician machine-checked one of the 372 claimed results in OpenAI's October 2026 mathematics release, the L³ boundedness of the trilinear Hilbert transform with slopes 1, 2 and 3, writing the theorem statement by hand and having coding agents generate roughly 194,000 lines of Lean proof from a blueprint another model wrote. OpenAI's release carried an L³ bound for the trilinear Hilbert transform with fixed slopes 1, 2 and 3 as family 086, published on 2026-10-05 with no formalization attached. Joris Roos stated the theorem and the operator by hand in Lean 4 against Mathlib, as an a priori estimate on Schwartz functions, then had coding agents prove it from a blueprint that GPT-6 Astra Pro generated from the OpenAI manuscript and from a shorter version of the argument the same model produced. The proof runs to about 194,000 lines over 61 files, built between 8 and 16 October, first by Codex with GPT-6 Astra Light and then by Claude Opus 5.5; machine-generated code is confined to an Auto namespace and directory, and the README is human-written. The author records that Claude at medium reasoning effort stalled without disclosing it, building redundant wrappers and revisiting the same parts of the blueprint, which human monitoring of an agent-maintained status file caught and a large refactor at higher effort repaired. The Comparator challenge file states the theorem with its proof omitted and a solution module supplies it, permitting only propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice. Lab: Independent. Model: GPT-6 Astra Pro for the blueprint, with GPT-6 Astra Light and Claude Opus 5.5 autoformalizing the proof. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Claude-designed protein binders against five scorpion neurotoxins
item.description: A generative design campaign run by an internal Anthropic model produced 318,484 candidate proteins against five scorpion-venom neurotoxins; of the 211 that were synthesised and tested, 17 met the binding criterion at both contract laboratories, the tightest at single-digit nanomolar affinity, and none was tested for venom neutralisation. Anthropic's initial prompt named five neurotoxins from four regions, Cn2 from Centruroides noxius in Mexico, Ts1 from Brazil, AaH I and AaH II from North Africa and LqhIII from the Middle East, along with the protein design and folding tools to use and the rules for novelty, scoring and filtering. The model chose the target structures from the PDB and the AlphaFold database, picked five hotspots per toxin, set its own quality thresholds, drove 12 design tools to 318,484 designs and co-folded 553,052 design-toxin pairs, using on the order of 10,000 GPU hours. It selected 180 designs for synthesis 64 hours after the first prompt, and 31 more were added with its help, for 211 tested in total. Of those, 17 met the hit criterion: binding in every replicate at both laboratories with every dissociation constant at 1 micromolar or tighter, and no signal against an off-target stickiness control. All 17 bound a single toxin, seven against Cn2, four against AaH II, four against AaH I and two against LqhIII, with Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2 in the single-digit nanomolar range, while every design intended to bind more than one toxin failed. Lab: Anthropic. Model: Internal Anthropic research model operating within Claude Science, not named or versioned in the post. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: Adapting an adult chest-radiograph model to neonatal intensive care across 30 units
item.description: A model trained to assess endotracheal tube position on adult chest radiographs was retrained in sequence at 30 neonatal intensive care units in 20 countries and territories, 50 radiographs per site and with no pooling of patient data, reaching a mean landmark localisation error of 0.67 cm against 1.29 cm for hospital-specific fine-tuning and 4.30 cm for the unadapted adult model. Fewer than one in five commercially available radiology AI models are cleared for paediatric use, models trained on adults generalise poorly to neonates, and neonatal images are scarce in public datasets, so the gap is usually closed by local data curation that most units cannot do. This international retrospective study evaluated continual learning as a privacy-preserving way to adapt an adult endotracheal-tube assessment model to neonatal care: each of 30 neonatal intensive care units across 20 countries and territories contributed 50 radiographs, and the model was retrained sequentially from site to site with no centralised pooling. Continual learning reached a mean anatomical landmark localisation error of 0.67 cm, against 1.29 cm for hospital-specific fine-tuning and 4.30 cm for the adult-only model, and was better at 29 of the 30 sites. Detection of deep intubations improved at 27 of 30 sites. The authors present this as evidence that collaborative learning without data sharing can address a paediatric deployment gap, not as a clinical outcome result. Lab: International NICU continual-learning consortium. Model: Adult endotracheal-tube assessment deep learning model adapted by continual learning; the base model is not named in the abstract. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Randomised trial of AI-supported diabetic retinopathy screening in Tanzania
item.description: In a randomised trial at 24 Tanzanian hospitals, giving people an AI screening result during the visit with face-to-face counselling roughly doubled the share of those with genuinely referable diabetic retinopathy who reached the referral eye clinic within eight weeks, from 18.2% to 35.9%. Non-attendance after referral is one of the main failure points of diabetic retinopathy screening programmes in Africa, and an AI grader can return a result during the screening visit rather than weeks later. This two-arm, parallel-group, individually randomised trial ran at non-communicable disease and diabetic clinics in 24 hospitals in the Kilimanjaro and Arusha regions between 8 March 2023 and 31 August 2024. Both arms had retinal photographs taken of both eyes; in the intervention arm the images went to the AI software and the participant was given a non-referable, referable or ungradable result with face-to-face counselling before leaving the photography room, and was referred if the output was referable or ungradable, while the standard-of-care arm received deferred human grading and a telephone result typically two to four weeks later. Of 2,378 participants enrolled, 1,192 were assigned to the AI arm and 1,186 to standard care, and 904 were classified by masked UK-certified graders as having true referable disease. Among those, attendance at the central ophthalmology clinic within eight weeks was 157 of 437 (35.9%) in the AI arm against 85 of 467 (18.2%) under standard care, an absolute difference of 17.7 percentage points (95% CI 12.0 to 23.4) and an odds ratio of 2.52 (95% CI 1.86 to 3.42), with p < 0.0001. Lab: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine / Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre. Model: Unknown. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Inpatient prototype of a conversational EEG device that retrains its own seizure detector
item.description: A prototype linking inpatient scalp and intracranial EEG to large language models let 13 epilepsy patients exchange messages with their monitoring system through a phone app, and the seizure-detection algorithms improved their precision over several days from that feedback without expert reprogramming. Implantable epilepsy devices can detect impending seizures, missed medication and impaired cognition, but have no way to tell the person carrying them in real time, which the authors describe as a limitation common to most medical devices. The prototype links scalp and intracranial EEG to secure large language models that communicate bidirectionally with patients through a smartphone app, with an AI agent consuming biomarkers of sleep, medication level, cognition and seizure risk extracted from brain activity. Either side can begin a conversation: the agent reports clinical events and physiological trends, records symptoms, responses and behaviours, and retrains itself on what it gathers. The authors demonstrate the platform in 13 patients undergoing inpatient video-EEG monitoring and report that seizure-detection algorithms optimised their precision over several days without expert intervention, which they contrast with the months of iterative in-person physician programming currently required. Patients rated the system highly usable and responded positively to messages about sleep, cognition and seizure risk, and the authors describe safeguards including efficient expert review for further fine-tuning and controls on communication content. Lab: University of Pennsylvania. Model: Unnamed secure large language models behind an AI agent; no vendor or version is given in the preprint abstract. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Erdős Problem 173: a two-coloring of the plane misses at most one triangle, which is equilateral
item.description: A Lean-checked proof that in every two-coloring of the plane, every triangle except possibly one equilateral triangle has a monochromatic congruent copy, settling a 1973 conjecture of Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus, found by GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 working in alternation. Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus conjectured in 1973 that every non-equilateral triangle has a monochromatic copy in every two-coloring of the plane, and gave the alternating-strip coloring that shows one equilateral triangle can be missed. Special cases were settled for right triangles by Shader in 1976, for colorings with closed or open classes by Jelínek, Kynčl, Stolař and Valla in 2009, and for further families by Currier, Moore and Yip in 2024. By the eight-point configuration of the 1975 sequel, it suffices to show that no coloring avoids the equilateral triangles of two different side lengths. The proof does this with a spectral argument for side ratios far from one, an irrational-rotation argument on circles for ratios near one, and a transfer from arbitrary to measurable colorings adapted from OpenAI's unrefereed preprint 'The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable', extended here from the algebraic numbers to the algebraic closure of ℚ(x) for every real x. Comparator checks five theorems, three of them, erdos_173 included, copied verbatim from Formal Conjectures. Lab: Plasma AI. Model: GPT-6 Astra (Codex) and Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Code), alternating; Claude Opus 5.5 (Lean formalization). Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Erdős Problem 111: graphs that are not countably colorable need superlinear deletions to become bipartite
item.description: A Lean-checked proof that if every finite subgraph on m vertices of a graph can be made bipartite by deleting at most Cm edges, the graph is countably colorable, so h_G(n)/n → ∞ for every graph of chromatic number ℵ₁, answering the second question of Erdős Problem 111; the proof was found by GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 in alternation. For a graph G, h_G(n) is the least number such that every subgraph on n vertices can be made bipartite by deleting at most h_G(n) edges. Erdős, Hajnal and Szemerédi showed that h_G(n) ≫ n for every graph of chromatic number ℵ₁ and built such graphs with h_G(n) ≤ 2n^(3/2), and Erdős asked whether h_G(n)/n → ∞. The proof builds random sign assignments along a continuous chain of closed vertex sets, forces each vertex with an infinite trace to oppose its derived sign, passes to limits along an ultrafilter, and splits the resulting signs, as unit vectors in L², into countably many classes within which greedy coloring succeeds. Per the repository, Claude Opus 5.5 wrote the first complete proof and GPT-6 Astra checked and revised it, and Claude Opus 5.5 then wrote the Lean. The first, open-ended question of the problem, the exact growth of h_G(n), is not addressed. Lab: Plasma AI. Model: GPT-6 Astra (Codex) and Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Code), alternating; Claude Opus 5.5 (Lean formalization). Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Erdős Problem 408: an unconditional normal order for the number of totient iterations
item.description: A Lean-checked proof that the least k with φₖ(n) = 1 has normal order α log n for a constant 1/log 3 ≤ α ≤ 1/log 2, answering the first two questions of Erdős Problem 408 without the Elliott-Halberstam hypothesis a 1990 proof needed, by building on OpenAI's unrefereed zero-free half-plane and shifted-prime results. Let f(n) be the least k ≥ 1 with φₖ(n) = 1. Pillai showed in 1929 that f(n) lies between about log n/log 3 and log n/log 2, and Erdős, Granville, Pomerance and Spiro proved in 1990 that it has normal order α log n conditionally on a form of the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture. This development removes the condition, with mean-square error O(x(log x)²/(log log x)⁵), so f(n)/log n tends to α on a set of density one and its distribution function is the point mass at α. The inputs that replace Elliott-Halberstam are OpenAI's zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8 for Dirichlet L-functions and the transference machinery of two OpenAI shifted-prime preprints of 24 September 2026, extended here. The Lean proofs of the half-plane, and Yao Xu's formalization of one of those preprints, are vendored and build with the project, so neither is assumed. The third, open-ended question of the problem is not formalized. Lab: Plasma AI. Model: Claude Opus 5.5 (Lean formalization); the argument is credited to Plasma AI without naming a model. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Pointwise convergence of ergodic averages along two commuting transformations
item.description: A Lean-checked proof that for two commuting measure-preserving transformations T and S of a probability space, the averages N⁻¹∑_(n < N)f(Tⁿx) g(Sⁿx) converge almost everywhere whenever f ∈ Lᵖ and g ∈ L^q with 1/p + 1/q ≤ 1, found by a model asked to adapt OpenAI's recent triangular Hilbert transform result. Norm convergence of these bilinear averages has been known since Conze and Lesigne in the 1980s. Pointwise convergence was known when one transformation is a power of the other, by Bourgain's double recurrence theorem, and for distal systems by Donoso and Sun; the general commuting case is the standing pointwise question, and the triangular Hilbert transform is the singular integral long studied as its harmonic-analysis counterpart. According to the repository, GPT-6 Astra Pro was instructed to adapt OpenAI's preprint 'Annular variation of the triangular Hilbert transform at the symmetric point', released on 5 October 2026, solved the problem and wrote a blueprint, and Claude Opus 5.5 then generated the Lean formalization. The statement in Theorems.lean, written by the human authors, uses only Mathlib's definitions of measure-preserving maps, Lᵖ membership and limits, and the Palomar record replays the proof against it under the three standard axioms. Lab: Independent. Model: GPT-6 Astra Pro (proof and blueprint); Claude Opus 5.5 (Lean formalization). Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: NIST elliptic-curve seeds traced to a 1990s C random number generator seeded with the clock
item.description: An Anthropic model showed that the published seeds of the NIST prime curves P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 and five ANSI X9.62 example curves are outputs of the C library's lrand48 generator seeded with Unix timestamps from May 1997 to April 1998, not hashes of a secret phrase, answering the origin question behind a long-standing backdoor debate. The NIST curves standardised around 2000 were said to be generated verifiably at random from SHA-1 hashes of seeds, but the seeds themselves were unexplained, which fed long-running suspicion that they had been chosen to target weak curves; Jerry Solinas's recollection that they came from hashing a humorous phrase was never confirmed, and in 2023 Filippo Valsorda offered a bounty for an explanation. The announcement says an employee asked an internal research model to work out how the seeds were generated, without the phrase clue, and that it identified lrand48 in under half an hour. Each prime-curve seed is a run of lrand48 outputs shifted right by 23 bits from a generator seeded with a 1997 or 1998 timestamp: P-256's is the 1,842nd 20-byte candidate of a run started at 01:52:34 UTC on 16 August 1997. Four binary-curve seeds fit lrand48 seeded with half the timestamp, and the base points of P-192 and five X9.62 curves come from the random number generator of Arjen Lenstra's FreeLIP library. Lab: Anthropic. Model: Internal Anthropic research model (Claude), not named in the announcement. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: LLM-designed quantum circuits with fewer gates and qubits than published designs in seven of eight tasks
item.description: Claude, run in a loop with an automated evaluator, produced reversible circuits that cut both Toffoli and qubit counts below the best published designs in seven of eight quantum-computing primitives and found a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion in the eighth, including an elliptic-curve point addition with 17 times fewer gates at 12% more qubits. The tasks span numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation and number theory, and each was posed as a plain-language specification with an external program that checks a circuit's correctness and scores it by qubits times gates. Claude proposed designs, received the score and revised, with no human input between rounds. For elliptic-curve point addition, the core step of quantum discrete-logarithm attacks, it found a reversible implementation of the divsteps modular-inversion algorithm that stores no branch history, checked the key identity by simulation and in Lean, and extended the Pareto frontier against Schrottenloher's and Luo and colleagues' 2026 designs. For the Reed-Solomon decoder inside Decoded Quantum Interferometry, the announcement reports about 12 times fewer gates than Google's construction and a locator step needing 19 qubits instead of a worst-case 665, tested on 403 million sample decodings with a failure rate of about one in 10,000. Lab: Anthropic. Model: Claude (the announcement names Claude Mythos 5). Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Search scaffold.

item.title: Randomised trial of AI wearable monitoring after heart-failure discharge finds no fall in rehospitalisation (LINK-HF2)
item.description: In a randomised trial of 171 veterans discharged after a heart-failure admission at five VA medical centres, alerts from a personalised AI model reading a wearable patch, routed to clinicians with a response algorithm, were feasible but did not reduce heart-failure rehospitalisation (16.3% against 18.7%, hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.84) or a composite of rehospitalisation, emergency visits and death. LINK-HF2 was a prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint study. All participants wore a continuous multisensor patch for up to 90 days; in the intervention arm a similarity-based model learned each patient's baseline cardiorespiratory and activity signals and notified clinicians of deviations, and clinicians responded within a median of one day. Median adherence to the patch was 72.4% of follow-up days. The intervention arm had fewer AI-detected episodes of physiological instability (hazard ratio 0.76, P = 0.025), but neither heart-failure rehospitalisation nor the composite of all-cause unplanned rehospitalisation, emergency visits and death moved (hazard ratio 1.03). Interviews named workflow integration and uncertainty about how to respond as the main barriers. It follows the 2020 LINK-HF study, in which the same approach detected precursors of heart-failure rehospitalisation with 76% to 88% sensitivity. Lab: US Department of Veterans Affairs / University of Utah. Model: Personalised similarity-based anomaly model on wearable multisensor data, not named in the abstract. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Pragmatic randomised trial of AI-triggered decision support for postoperative delirium finds no effect
item.description: In a pragmatic trial embedded in routine care at Mount Sinai, 7,294 surgical patients flagged as cognitively impaired by a natural-language-processing model, test scores or diagnosis codes were randomised to a non-interruptive decision-support nudge for anaesthesia teams or usual care, with no difference in postoperative delirium (35.1% against 32.7%, P = 0.37) or in adherence to 12 best practices, though fewer than one in five patients were ever assessed for delirium. Patients with preoperative cognitive impairment, identified immediately before surgery by a validated natural-language-processing algorithm over the electronic health record, Mini-Mental State Examination scores or diagnostic codes, were randomised between June 2023 and August 2024 either to a non-interruptive decision-support intervention in the record, prompting anaesthesia teams toward perioperative best practices, or to routine care. The primary outcome was delirium within seven days on the 4 A's Test. Only 1,255 of 7,294 patients (17.2%) had a documented assessment, of whom 34% developed delirium, with no difference between arms, and none of the 12 best-practice adherence measures differed either. The authors conclude that inconsistent routine delirium screening limits what the trial can say about whether the intervention works. Lab: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. Model: Natural-language-processing model for cognitive impairment in health records, not named in the abstract. Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Lambert series values, including the Erdős-Borwein constant, are not quadratic irrationals
item.description: A self-published paper with a Lean formalization claims that F(q) = ∑_(n ≥ 1)1/(qⁿ − 1) is neither rational nor quadratic irrational for every integer q ≥ 2, the Erdős-Borwein constant F(2) included, and widens the region where F(a/b) is known to be irrational from log b/log a < 0.405683 to log b/log a < 0.5728, with generative AI credited with nearly all of the mathematics. Erdős proved in 1948 that F(q) is irrational for integer q ≥ 2, and Erdős Problem 1049, a conjecture of Chowla, asks for irrationality at every rational base t > 1. The paper proves a degree-exclusion theorem for every real algebraic base: if eλ log M(q) < log q, with λ ≈ 0.4272 and M(q) the Mahler measure, then F(q) satisfies no polynomial relation of degree at most e over ℚ(q). The argument builds Gram determinants that are strictly positive at the true value and decay exponentially in N³, clears their cyclotomic denominators without losing the decay, and closes with the product formula. For rational bases this widens the irrationality region from Cook's 2026 threshold of 0.405683 to 0.5728, or 0.573290 with a refinement that is formalized but only remarked on in the paper. Problem 1049 itself stays open, since bases such as 3/2 fall outside the region. Lab: Independent. Model: Generative AI, not named in the repository. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: Counterexamples to Zak's modified integer round-down conjecture for the skiving stock problem
item.description: A self-published paper claims that the additive integrality gap of the skiving stock (bin covering) problem's pattern LP relaxations is unbounded, refuting Zak's 2003 conjecture that it always stays below two, by transferring OpenAI's unrefereed bin-packing construction; it states that the proof was generated by Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-5.6 Sol Pro. The skiving stock problem, called bin covering in the algorithms literature, asks for the most disjoint groups of items whose sizes each reach a threshold. Zak conjectured in 2003 that the gap between the standard pattern LP relaxation and the integer optimum is always less than two, the covering counterpart of the modified integer round-up property for cutting stock. The paper maps OpenAI's bin-packing instances of 24 September 2026, which have unbounded configuration-LP gaps, to covering instances by the complement bᵢ = 2 − aᵢ with threshold 9, and proves that saturation of the packing LP carries both LP values across while a covering deficit d becomes a packing excess of at most ⌈3d/2⌉. It concludes that the gaps of both the ordinary and the stronger proper relaxation are unbounded, and that distinguishing instances that cover B bins from those that cannot cover B − c is NP-hard for every fixed c. Lab: Independent. Model: Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-5.6 Sol Pro. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: Physicians steered by a covertly adversarial chatbot made harmful decisions at 49% of targeted points, against 2% with an aligned one
item.description: In a participant-blinded randomised experiment, 225 neurocritical-care physicians from 42 countries worked through anonymised real cases with a chatbot covertly instructed to steer them either toward predefined harmful options or toward correct ones; the adversarial version raised harmful decisions from 2% to 49% of targeted decision points and cut correct ones from 83% to 25%, and only two physicians reported suspecting manipulation. Thirty cases were built from real admissions to a quaternary neurocritical-care unit, each with four sequential decision points: differential diagnosis, primary diagnosis, diagnostic test and treatment. Expert consensus fixed a correct set at each point and, at 83 of the 120 points, a distinct harmful target. Each physician completed four cases, two in each mode in randomised order, with the same open-weight model, DeepSeek V4 Flash, differing between modes only in a case-specific system instruction; physicians recorded a draft decision, received the AI's feedback, could continue the dialogue and then locked a final decision. Across 2,485 targeted decision points the adjusted difference in harmful decisions was 47 percentage points (95% CI 43 to 51), with no clear protection from clinical experience, and of the 190 physicians who made a harmful decision under adversarial AI, 141 reported nothing unusual about it. Decisions were classified by two language models under blinding, with a third model and human adjudication for disagreements, checked against blinded expert consensus. Lab: University of California, San Francisco / Université Libre de Bruxelles. Model: DeepSeek V4 Flash. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: No zeros of any Dedekind zeta function with real part above 31/32, machine-checked in Lean
item.description: A Lean-formalized proof generated by Axiom Math's AxiomProver under two investigators' direction shows that for every number field K the Dedekind zeta function ζ_K(s) has no zeros with ℜs > 31/32. The manuscript takes its strategy from OpenAI's Artin manuscript (2026-10-06-artin-primitive-root), which claims a zero-free strip ℜs > 1 − 10⁻⁶ for finite-order Hecke L-functions over cyclotomic fields containing the twelfth roots of unity, and extends it to every number field with the wider half-plane ℜs > 31/32. It says the hardest part was formalizing Kazhdan and Patterson's metaplectic forms over number fields containing the twelfth roots of unity; abelian descent then reaches arbitrary number fields, and the Hecke corollary follows by factoring ζ_L for the cyclic extension L/K cut out by the character. For K = ℚ the half-plane is narrower than the 7/8 that 2026-10-06-quasi-riemann-hypothesis claims for the Riemann zeta function, but the result covers every number field and, unlike the OpenAI manuscripts it builds on, carries a third-party registration. The Lean statement is anchored on Mathlib's own NumberField.dedekindZeta: it asserts a function holomorphic away from s = 1 that agrees with ζ_K for ℜs > 1 and does not vanish for ℜs > 31/32, which by uniqueness of analytic continuation is the continued zeta function. The repository credits code adapted from openai/math, Tau Ceti and LeanPool, and vendors a class field theory development from the Palomar archive. A corollary extending the half-plane to every finite-order Hecke L-function over K, wherever it is holomorphic, is also formalized and registered, against a definition of ray class characters written in the challenge file. Lab: Axiom Math. Model: AxiomProver. Verification: Formally verified. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: Lower bound of 21 multiplications for 3×3 matrix multiplication over every field, with a Lean proof
item.description: Andrey Ivanov, working with OpenAI models through ChatGPT and Codex, claims that every exact bilinear algorithm for multiplying two 3 × 3 matrices over any field uses at least 21 multiplications, with a Palomar-registered Lean proof, which would raise the bound that holds over every field from Bläser's 19 of 2003. The bilinear complexity, or tensor rank, of 3 × 3 matrix multiplication sits below Laderman's 1976 algorithm with 23 multiplications, which works over every field, and over every field the best lower bound was Bläser's 19 from 2003. During 2026 a run of field-specific results closed the gap over 𝔽₂: 21 by Chengu Wang, 22 over 𝔽₂ and for integer coefficients by Rudich and Rousseau, and the exact rank 23 by Tomar on 2026-10-08, each by exhaustive or certified search tied to the field. This result is uniform: the Lean theorem takes any field K, any finite index set I, arbitrary linear forms aᵢ and bᵢ and matrices Wᵢ with AB = ∑ᵢaᵢ(A)bᵢ(B)Wᵢ for all A and B, and concludes |I| ≥ 21, with no assumption of minimality, nonzero terms or coefficient ranks. The argument passes to an algebraic closure, picks a decomposition minimizing a rank sum in its first coefficient family, and rules out 20 or fewer terms through what the author calls conductor growth and residual reconstruction. It concerns exact bilinear complexity, not border rank or the asymptotic exponent. Lab: Independent. Model: OpenAI models through ChatGPT and Codex, versions not recorded in the repository (GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Sol by the author's later account to vibemathed). Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: Collaborative.

item.title: Strict Pólya inequalities claimed for simply connected planar domains, Dirichlet and Neumann, with Lean formalizations
item.description: Quanyu Tang and Zuoqin Wang, working with ChatGPT, claim Pólya's 1954 eigenvalue conjecture in strict form for the Dirichlet Laplacian on every bounded simply connected planar domain and for the Neumann Laplacian on every bounded simply connected planar Lipschitz domain, with Palomar-registered Lean formalizations of both. Pólya conjectured that the Dirichlet eigenvalues of a planar domain of area |Ω| satisfy λⱼ(Ω) ≥ 4πj/|Ω| and the Neumann eigenvalues μⱼ(Ω) ≤ 4πj/|Ω|, the bounds that Weyl's law approaches from either side; it was proved for domains that tile the plane and is open for general domains. The Dirichlet paper proves |Ω|λⱼ(Ω) > 4πj for every j ≥ 1 on every bounded simply connected planar domain, with no boundary regularity, through a unitary boundary-transport formulation of the Helmholtz equation that relates Dirichlet resonances to eigenphase crossings via the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map: an exact area identity gives the sharp Weyl coefficient, a Ky Fan estimate leaves a strictly positive remainder, and conformal exhaustion handles general domains. The Neumann result proves |Ω|μⱼ(Ω) < 4πj for j ≥ 1 on bounded simply connected Lipschitz domains, indexed from μ₀ = 0, together with the equivalent counting form; its manuscript is not yet on arXiv, and a draft sits in the registered repository. Before this the conjecture was known for tiling domains, disks and a few further families such as annuli, and on 2026-10-05 Speciel proved two thirds of the Dirichlet bound for every planar domain. The two Lean developments are about 27,000 and 100,000 lines. Lab: Independent. Model: ChatGPT for the mathematics, version not stated; Aristotle (Harmonic) and Codex for the Lean. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: AMIE with real patients before urgent primary care visits: a prospective feasibility study
item.description: In a single-arm study at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, 98 patients completed a text conversation with Google's AMIE in the five days before an urgent primary care visit, under live physician supervision; no conversation needed a safety stop under prespecified criteria, supervisors noted one hallucination, and physicians found the transcript helpful for preparation in 33 of the 44 cases where they reviewed it. Adults with a single-complaint urgent appointment talked with AMIE beforehand, and the transcript and a summary went to their physician before the visit. 114 patients were enrolled between April and November 2025. Physician safety supervisors watched every conversation and were trained to intervene on predefined criteria; they intervened to add clinical information in five conversations. Clinical evaluators rated AMIE's conversations favourably in 87% to 100% of cases across 17 criteria, and patients in 48% to 96% across 16. Patients' attitudes towards AI improved after the conversation and stayed higher after their visit. Physicians returned surveys in 60 of 98 cases, read the transcript in 44, and said it might have changed their behaviour in 25. Funded by Alphabet. Lab: Google / Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. Model: AMIE (Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Truly subquadratic 3SUM and truly subcubic APSP, refuting two central fine-grained complexity hypotheses
item.description: A preprint by Josh Alman and Virginia Vassilevska Williams gives deterministic algorithms that solve 3SUM on polynomially bounded integers in time O(n^1.9992) and all-pairs shortest paths with polynomially bounded integer weights in time O(n^2.9995), refuting the 3SUM and APSP hypotheses, from an algorithm the paper says an internal Anthropic model found on its own. Both hypotheses say the textbook algorithms are essentially optimal: 3SUM, deciding whether three of n integers sum to zero, needs time n^(2 − o(1)), and APSP needs n^(3 − o(1)). Fine-grained complexity has used them, together with the Exact Triangle hypothesis, as the starting points of many conditional lower bounds, and the abstract describes these as the first polynomial improvements over the textbook algorithms. Everything follows from one new algorithm for thin matrix products: for an N × D integer matrix X and a D × N matrix Y with D ≤ N^(1/18), it computes the entries of XY at any set of at most N²/√D prescribed positions in O(N²/D^0.063) operations, by modifying a variant of Coppersmith's rectangular matrix multiplication algorithm built on a ten-multiplication identity of Schönhage. Read as a graph algorithm, it finds all triangles in sparse lopsided tripartite graphs in truly subquadratic time, and known reductions carry that to Exact Triangle, 3SUM and APSP, and further to the real-valued versions of 3SUM and APSP, the Zero-Weight k-Clique hypotheses and three hinted Online Matrix-Vector conjectures. According to the paper's methodology section, an Anthropic employee had an internal research model working on cryptographic constructions based on the average-case hardness of Zero-k-Clique; asked to verify and improve them, it instead developed this algorithm, first for the average case and then for the worst case, in one session of 16 million output tokens with no human input. Anthropic shared it with the authors in September 2026, and they simplified, strengthened and extended it and derived the further consequences. After the paper was written, an internal Anthropic model produced a Lean 4 formalization of five headline running-time claims on a word RAM defined in Lean. Lab: Anthropic. Model: Unreleased internal Anthropic research model (Claude), not named in the paper. Verification: Author verified. Autonomy: AI-led.

item.title: 36 manuscripts across 18 fields from the BootLoops harness run with Claude
item.description: Matthew Schwartz's open-source BootLoops harness, operated by Claude, produced 36 manuscripts with 19 coauthors between July and September 2026, mostly exact or certified computations carried from physics and computer science into fields such as population genetics, phylogenetics, ecology and health policy; eight are still in preparation and none is yet listed as published in a journal. BootLoops pools programs from particle physics, experimental mathematics, computer algebra and numerical analysis in one toolkit that a language-model agent can operate and extend. The overview paper (arXiv:2610.02286) says the computations were run by Claude with a human setting the targets and the standards, and that the package itself was written by AI apart from forks of public codes. The essay on Anthropic's blog counts 36 manuscripts in 18 fields with 19 coauthors over three months, chosen from about 400 candidate problems; the project's manuscript index lists the overview and 35 papers in nine groups, eight marked in preparation, and says every manuscript has been read by humans for accuracy, that many were drafted first by language models, and that those not yet fully checked are watermarked preliminary. The recurring move is to replace an estimate by an exact or certified answer: Feynman integrals in closed form by bootstrap, Bayesian evidence for four- and five-species phylogenetic trees as exact rational numbers, the site-frequency spectrum of a selected allele at any selection strength, Medicare star-rating cut points at the true optimum of their clustering criterion, and exact operating characteristics of published adaptive trial designs. Coauthors include Scott Edwards and Paul Lewis on phylogenetics, Michael Desai on population genetics, James O'Dwyer on ecology and Isaiah Andrews on economics. This registry's 2026-10-01-anisotropic-watson-integral is one result from the project. Lab: Independent. Model: Claude (the essay names Claude Fable 5 for the initial porting; versions per result are not recorded). Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Huang-Jiang-Oblomkov conjecture for a = 3: a new infinite family of Rogers-Ramanujan identities, with a Lean certificate conditional on eight literature facts
item.description: Kenny Lau and Ken Ono prove the a = 3 layer of the Huang-Jiang-Oblomkov conjecture, which equates a count of commuting nilpotent matrix pairs with X³ = Yᵇ over finite fields with an explicit theta quotient, giving a new infinite family of Rogers-Ramanujan identities; AxiomProver produced a Lean certificate of the deduction from eight cited literature facts. For coprime 1 < a < b, Huang, Jiang and Oblomkov assembled the normalized counts of commuting nilpotent n × n matrix pairs over 𝔽_q with Xᵃ = Yᵇ into a q-series Z_(a, b)(q) and conjectured that it equals an explicit product P_(a, b)(q) built from Jacobi's theta function and Dedekind's eta function, which would make the point count essentially a modular function on Γ(a + b). The conjecture is layered in a: the a = 2 layer is classical, containing the Rogers-Ramanujan and Andrews-Gordon identities, and the abstract says nothing was known for a ≥ 3. This paper proves the a = 3 layer in full, which the abstract describes as a new infinite family of Rogers-Ramanujan identities and a geometric origin for Warnaar's products. A companion paper by Huang, Lau, Ono and Paule (arXiv:2608.15219) proves the cases (a, b) = (3, 4), (3, 5), (3, 7) and (3, 8) through a finer sum-to-sum identity, and 2026-09-17-rogers-ramanujan-torus-knot later claims every coprime pair, which contains this layer. Lab: Axiom Math. Model: AxiomProver. Verification: Claimed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Cluster-randomised trial of an LLM decision-support tool in Kenyan primary care finds no reduction in treatment failure
item.description: In a pragmatic trial at 16 Penda Health clinics in Kenya, clinical officers randomised to a GPT-4o-based decision-support tool in the medical record saw 14-day treatment failure in 2.2% of 4,693 patients against 2.0% of 4,654 without it, an adjusted odds ratio of 0.77 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.08); the tool was safe but did not significantly reduce treatment failure. AI Consult is built into the cloud medical record Penda Health uses and reviews the clinician's notes, diagnosis and treatment at decision points. 103 clinical officers, the diploma-trained clinicians who staff much of Kenyan primary care, were randomised: 52 with the tool and 51 without. 9,691 patients were enrolled between April and July 2025. The primary outcome was an expert-adjudicated composite of treatment failure within 14 days. No serious adverse event was judged related to the tool, and independent review of adverse events found no safety signal. The trial was funded by the Gates Foundation and registered with the Pan-African Clinical Trials Registry (202502499779176). An earlier 2025 quality-improvement study at 15 Penda clinics, run with OpenAI, reported 16% fewer diagnostic errors and 13% fewer treatment errors across 39,849 visits by clinicians who had the tool, as rated by independent physicians; that measured errors in documented care, a different and softer outcome than this trial's. Lab: KEMRI-Wellcome Trust Research Programme / Penda Health / PATH. Model: AI Consult (GPT-4o). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Multicenter prospective validation of Epic's retrained sepsis model (version 2)
item.description: Epic's retrained sepsis model, gradient-boosted trees fine-tuned on each hospital's own data, discriminated sepsis at encounter-level AUROCs of 0.82 to 0.92 across 227,091 inpatient encounters at four large US health systems, in line with or above the 0.83 to 0.86 Epic reports internally, but with positive predictive values of only 0.13 to 0.26 and a high alert burden. Version 2, released in 2022, replaced the penalized logistic regression of version 1, addressed the methodological criticisms raised against it, and lets each site fine-tune on its own historical data. Investigators at four health systems collected data for a consecutive period right after each site went live, between August 2023 and March 2025, and scored the model against Sepsis-3 criteria; 7,401 of the 227,091 encounters (3.3%) met them. At the prediction level, with a 12-hour horizon, AUROC ranged from 0.75 to 0.85; measured against clinicians' own recognition of sepsis (antibiotic, lactate and culture orders), encounter-level AUROC was 0.80 to 0.90. According to Epic, as cited in the paper, 95 organisations representing 731 hospitals used version 2 as of August 2025, while more than 100 organisations still ran version 1. Lab: Epic Systems. Model: Epic Sepsis Model v2 (gradient-boosted trees with local fine-tuning). Verification: Independently checked. Autonomy: AI-assisted.

item.title: Randomised trial of AI-supported mammography screening in 105,934 women (MASAI)
item.description: In a Swedish screening trial that randomised 105,934 women, AI triage and detection support found 29% more cancers than standard double reading, cut radiologists' reading workload by 44%, and met its primary endpoint of a non-inferior interval cancer rate, 1.55 against 1.76 per 1,000, with sensitivity of 80.5% against 73.8% at the same 98.5% specificity. Women screened at four sites in southwest Sweden between April 2021 and December 2022 were randomised 1:1. In the AI arm, Transpara gave each examination a malignancy risk score from 1 to 10: scores 1 to 9 went to a single radiologist and score 10 to two, and radiologists saw the scores and, for high scores, the system's marks on suspicious areas. The control arm was the Swedish standard of independent double reading without AI. Results came in three papers. A 2023 safety analysis of the first 80,033 women (Lancet Oncology) found the AI arm safe, with a 44.3% lower reading workload. A 2025 analysis of all participants (Lancet Digital Health) found 338 cancers against 262, a detection rate of 6.4 against 5.0 per 1,000 (ratio 1.29), mostly small node-negative invasive cancers, with no significant rise in recalls or false positives and 61,248 against 109,692 screen readings. The 2026 primary-endpoint paper (The Lancet) reports interval cancers, those surfacing between screening rounds: a proportion ratio of 0.88 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.18) within a 20% non-inferiority margin, with descriptively fewer invasive (75 against 89), large (38 against 48) and non-luminal A (43 against 59) interval cancers. Lab: Lund University. Model: Transpara 1.7.0 (ScreenPoint Medical). Verification: Peer reviewed. Autonomy: AI-assisted.
